analysis.one_liner: Creates a Justice, FTC, and Agriculture task force to investigate price gouging and food-industry consolidation.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote; after being referred to three House committees and a subcommittee, it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a standing task force of officials from the Department of Justice, the Federal Trade Commission, and the Department of Agriculture focused on unfair and illegal pricing that raises costs for American families. The task force would investigate anticompetitive and deceptive business practices that raise prices, work to prevent consolidation in the food sector, counteract food price manipulation along the supply chain, and report to Congress every 90 days on its findings, federal spending effects on food prices, and input costs for producers, manufacturers, and retailers. It is an advisory body: it recommends legislation and reports findings, but cannot itself fine companies or cap prices. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be consumers squeezed by grocery and other prices, plus farmers and small producers who would gain a task force analyzing input costs and pushing back against consolidation in the food sector that squeezes both shoppers and suppliers. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: Creates a multi-agency task force charged with investigating and recommending ways to stop anticompetitive, unfair, deceptive, or fraudulent practices that increase prices for American families. [S2]

Directs the task force to recommend legislation to prevent consolidation in the food sector and counteract food price manipulation throughout the supply chain, and to report to Congress every 90 days on its work. [S2]
Requires the task force to analyze input costs for producers, manufacturers, and retailers, which would surface where margin pressures and pricing power sit along the food supply chain. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall on federal agencies, which would need to staff and run the task force, and potentially on large food companies that could face investigations into pricing and consolidation. There is no direct tax or fee on the public in the bill. [S2]
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal agencies and large food companies

drawbacks.text: The task force is advisory only: it can investigate and recommend legislation, but it has no power to fine companies, cap prices, or file cases on its own, so its value depends entirely on what Congress does with its recommendations. [S2]

A standing price-gouging task force could generate recurring public reports accusing firms of 'price manipulation' or 'fraudulent practices' without clear legal definitions in the bill, creating pressure on businesses whose pricing is lawful but unpopular. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a low-cost, low-risk step: it creates an investigative body and reporting requirements rather than price controls, so it poses little downside beyond agency staffing and the possibility of politically charged reports. Its limits are the flip side of its modest design: it cannot stop gouging itself, only recommend steps for Congress to take. Its fate was decided not by its merits but by the fact that it was a freshman-level effort with one cosponsor that never advanced in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then a subcommittee, and no committee ever reported it out, so it sat until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the bill on May 22, 2024. [S1]
It had one cosponsor, a Democrat. [S3]
It was referred to the Judiciary, Agriculture, and Energy and Commerce committees, then on May 24, 2024, to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce. [S4]
No committee reported the bill and no vote ever occurred in either chamber; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food companies and retailers that might have faced investigations into pricing and consolidation were spared the scrutiny the task force would have brought; consumers gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Angie Craig
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary, Agriculture, and Energy and Commerce committees.

for.name: House Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 22, 2024, and sent it to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce; never held a markup or reported it out.

against.name: House Agriculture and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for their jurisdictions on May 22, 2024, and took no action on it.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters were Democrats and there is no record of Republican support; the bill received no votes, so no roll-call breakdown exists. [S3]

industries.industry: Large food retailers and grocery chains
industries.note: The task force would investigate pricing practices along the food supply chain and recommend ways to counteract food price manipulation, with retailers a natural focus since they set shelf prices families pay. [S2]

The bill targets consolidation and supply-chain manipulation, which would put concentrated meatpacking and manufacturing sectors under scrutiny, but it also requires analysis of their input costs, which could support arguments that narrow margins rather than greed drive prices. [S2]
The task force would analyze producer input costs and push to prevent consolidation in the food sector, which many farm groups view as squeezing growers between dominant buyers and sellers. [S2]
